cemc-fryer-2010-01a.title: Fit the staircases together
cemc-fryer-2010-01a.body:
The left piece is a "staircase" with rows of 1, 2, 3, 4 tiles (all flush on the right), and the right piece is a staircase with rows of 1, 2, 3 tiles (flush on the left).

The empty space above the left piece (inside a $4 \times 4$ square) is a staircase with rows of 3, 2, 1 tiles, flush on the left. Turn the right piece a quarter turn clockwise: it becomes exactly this shape. Slide it into the gap: its row of 3 sits beside the left piece's top tile, its row of 2 beside the row of 2, and its single tile beside the row of 3. Every row then has 4 tiles:

| Row | from left piece | from right piece | total |
|---|---|---|---|
| top | 1 | 3 | 4 |
| 2nd | 2 | 2 | 4 |
| 3rd | 3 | 1 | 4 |
| bottom | 4 | 0 | 4 |

This is a $4 \times 4$ square of 16 tiles.

cemc-fryer-2010-01b.title: Add a new bottom row
cemc-fryer-2010-01b.body:
Figure 5 is Figure 4 with a new bottom row of $7 + 2 = 9$ tiles: $1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 25$ tiles.

**Answer: 25**

cemc-fryer-2010-01b.title: Make a square
cemc-fryer-2010-01b.body:
Cutting and rearranging as in part (a), Figure 5 becomes a $5 \times 5$ square, so it has 25 tiles.

**Answer: 25**

cemc-fryer-2010-01c.title: Continue the pattern
cemc-fryer-2010-01c.body:
The bottom rows have $1, 3, 5, 7, 9, \dots$ tiles, going up by 2 each time. Figure 10's bottom row has $1 + 9 \times 2 = 19$ tiles.

**Answer: 19**

cemc-fryer-2010-01d.title: Two extra rows
cemc-fryer-2010-01d.body:
Figure 11 is Figure 9 plus two more rows: the bottom rows of Figure 10 (19 tiles) and Figure 11 ($19 + 2 = 21$ tiles). The difference is $19 + 21 = 40$.

**Answer: 40**

cemc-fryer-2010-01d.title: Squares
cemc-fryer-2010-01d.body:
As in part (a), Figure $n$ rearranges into an $n \times n$ square. So the difference is $11^2 - 9^2 = 121 - 81 = 40$.

**Answer: 40**

cemc-fryer-2010-02a.title: Symmetry
cemc-fryer-2010-02a.body:
The numbers are evenly spaced around 73 ($73 \pm 1$, $73 \pm 2$), so their average is the middle number, 73.

**Answer: 73**

cemc-fryer-2010-02bii.title: Compute the average
cemc-fryer-2010-02bii.body: The average is $\frac{5n + 10}{5} = n + 2$. Adding 2 does not change whether a number is odd or even, so $n + 2$ is odd exactly when $n$ is odd. Hence if the average is odd, $n$ is odd. ∎

cemc-fryer-2010-02c.title: Compute the average
cemc-fryer-2010-02c.body: The sum is $6n + 15$, so the average is $\frac{6n + 15}{6} = n + \frac52 = (n + 2) + \frac12$. This is always halfway between two integers, so it is never an integer. ∎

cemc-fryer-2010-02c.title: Parity of the sum
cemc-fryer-2010-02c.body: For the average to be an integer, the sum $6n + 15$ would have to be a multiple of 6, in particular even. But $6n$ is even and 15 is odd, so $6n + 15$ is odd. ∎

cemc-fryer-2010-03a.title: Distance = speed × time
cemc-fryer-2010-03a.body:
In 9 hours at 60 km/h, Train 1 travels $540$ km. This is $\frac23$ of the whole distance, so $\frac13$ is 270 km and the whole distance is $3 \times 270 = 810$ km.

**Answer: 810 km**

cemc-fryer-2010-03a.title: Total time
cemc-fryer-2010-03a.body:
If $\frac23$ of the trip takes 9 hours, the whole trip takes $9 \div \frac23 = 13.5$ hours, so the distance is $60 \times 13.5 = 810$ km.

**Answer: 810 km**

cemc-fryer-2010-03b.title: Distance ÷ time
cemc-fryer-2010-03b.body:
$\frac23 \times 810 = 540$ km in 6 hours, so Train 2's speed is $540 \div 6 = 90$ km/h.

**Answer: 90 km/h**

cemc-fryer-2010-03c.title: Equation in Train 1's travel time
cemc-fryer-2010-03c.body:
Let Train 1 take $t$ hours to reach Cuford. Train 2 takes $t - 3\frac12$ hours. Their distances add up to 810 km:

$$60t + 90\left(t - \tfrac72\right) = 810 \implies 150t - 315 = 810 \implies t = 7\tfrac12.$$

Train 1 left $7\frac12$ hours before 9:00 p.m., at 1:30 p.m.

**Answer: 1:30 p.m.**

cemc-fryer-2010-03c.title: Head start
cemc-fryer-2010-03c.body:
In its $3\frac12$-hour head start, Train 1 covers $210$ km. The remaining $600$ km is closed by both trains together at $60 + 90 = 150$ km/h, taking 4 hours. So Train 1 travels $3\frac12 + 4 = 7\frac12$ hours, leaving at 1:30 p.m.

**Answer: 1:30 p.m.**

cemc-fryer-2010-04a.title: Count by number of digits
cemc-fryer-2010-04a.body:
- One digit: $1$–$9$: 9 palindromes.
- Two digits: $11, 22, \dots, 99$: 9 palindromes.
- Three digits: $aba$ with $a \in \{1, \dots, 9\}$, $b \in \{0, \dots, 9\}$: $9 \times 10 = 90$.

Total $9 + 9 + 90 = 108$.

**Answer: 108**

cemc-fryer-2010-04b.title: The first four digits decide
cemc-fryer-2010-04b.body:
A 7-digit palindrome has the form $abcdcba$, determined by $a$ (9 choices, not 0), $b$, $c$, $d$ (10 choices each): $9 \times 10 \times 10 \times 10 = 9000$.

**Answer: 9000**

cemc-fryer-2010-04c.title: Count in blocks
cemc-fryer-2010-04c.body:
Ordering the palindromes $abcdcba$ is the same as ordering the 4-digit strings $abcd$.

- Each first digit gives 1000 palindromes, so numbers 2001–3000 start with 3.
- Within those, $b = 0$ gives 100 (numbers 2001–2100), so the 2125th has $b = 1$; it is the 25th of the form $31cdc13$.
- $c = 0$ gives the 1st–10th, $c = 1$ the 11th–20th, $c = 2$ the 21st–30th. The 25th has $c = 2$ and is the 5th of those, so $d = 4$.

The palindrome is $3124213$.

**Answer: 3124213**

cemc-fryer-2010-04c.title: Translate the position into digits
cemc-fryer-2010-04c.body:
The $k$-th palindrome corresponds to the 4-digit number $abcd = 999 + k$ (the first is $1000 \to 1000001$). For $k = 2125$: $abcd = 3124$, giving $3124213$.

**Answer: 3124213**

cemc-fryer-2010-04d.title: Factor the place values
cemc-fryer-2010-04d.body:
A six-digit palindrome is $abccba = 100001a + 10010b + 1100c = 11(9091a + 910b + 100c)$, with $1 \le a \le 9$ and $0 \le b, c \le 9$.

Since $\gcd(11, 91) = 1$, it is divisible by 91 exactly when $k = 9091a + 910b + 100c$ is. Now

$$k = 91(100a + 10b + c) + 9(c - a),$$

so we need $91 \mid 9(c - a)$, i.e. $91 \mid c - a$. As $-9 \le c - a \le 8$, this means $c = a$.

So the palindromes are $abaaba$: 9 choices of $a$ and 10 of $b$, giving 90.

**Answer: 90**

cemc-fryer-2010-04d.title: Use 1001 = 7 × 11 × 13
cemc-fryer-2010-04d.body:
$91 = 7 \times 13$ and $1001 = 7 \times 11 \times 13$, so $1001 \equiv 0 \pmod{91}$, i.e. $1000 \equiv -1$. Write $abccba = 1000 \cdot \overline{abc} + \overline{cba} \equiv \overline{cba} - \overline{abc} = 99(c - a) \pmod{91}$.

Since $\gcd(99, 91) = 1$, we need $91 \mid c - a$, so $c = a$. That gives $9 \times 10 = 90$ palindromes.

**Answer: 90**
